IGCSE Physics - Chapter 2: Forces and Motion (Questions 1-8)

Question 1

(0625/41_Summer_2017_Q1) - Forces And Motion

Fig. 1.1 is the speed-time graph for an ice skater.

(a) Explain what is meant by deceleration. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

Deceleration is the rate of decrease of velocity or speed. It means the object is slowing down.

(b) Use Fig. 1.1 to determine

(i) the distance travelled between times t = 3.0s and t = 6.0s, [2]

Tap to reveal answer

The distance travelled is the area under the graph between the given times. This area can be calculated as a trapezium: Area = ½ × (a+b) × h = ½ × (11 m/s + 5 m/s) × 3.0 s = 24 m.

(ii) the deceleration between times t = 3.0s and t = 6.0s. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Deceleration is the gradient of the graph in this section. a = (change in velocity) ⁄ (time taken) = (5 m/s - 11 m/s) ⁄ (6.0 s - 3.0 s) = -6 m/s ⁄ 3.0 s. The deceleration is 2.0 m/s².

(c) (i) State what happens to the size of the deceleration after time t = 6.0 s. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

After t = 6.0 s, the size of the deceleration decreases.

(ii) State what happens to the resultant force on the skater after time t = 6.0 s. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

Since the deceleration is decreasing, the resultant force on the skater also decreases.

Question 2

(0625/42_Summer_2017_Q1) - Forces And Motion

(a) (i) Speed is a scalar quantity and velocity is a vector quantity. State how a scalar quantity differs from a vector quantity. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

A scalar quantity has magnitude only, while a vector quantity has both magnitude and direction.

(ii) Underline the two scalar quantities in the list below. [1]

energy     force     impulse     momentum     temperature

Tap to reveal answer

The two scalar quantities are energy and temperature.

(b) A boat is moving at constant speed. On Fig. 1.1, sketch a distance-time graph for the boat. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

The graph should be a straight line with a positive, non-zero gradient, starting from the origin.

(c) The boat in (b) is moving due west at a speed of 6.5 m/s relative to the water. The water is moving due south at 3.5m/s. In the space below, draw a scale diagram to determine the size and direction of the resultant of these two velocities. State the scale used. [4]

Tap to reveal answer

Using a scale diagram (e.g., 1 cm : 1 m/s), a right-angled vector triangle is drawn. The resultant velocity is the hypotenuse. The size of the resultant velocity is between 7.2-7.6 m/s. The direction is an angle between 26.0° and 30.5° south of west.

Question 3

(0625/43_Summer_2017_Q1) - Forces And Motion

(a) Acceleration is a vector quantity. Underline the two vector quantities in the list below. [1]

energy     force     frequency     impulse     mass     refractive index

Tap to reveal answer

The two vector quantities are force and impulse.

(b) A car accelerates uniformly from rest at 2.2 m/s² for 3.0s.

(i) Calculate the speed of the car at time t = 3.0 s. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Using the equation v = u + at, where u=0. The speed is v = 2.2 m/s² × 3.0 s = 6.6 m/s.

(ii) At time t = 3.0 s, it has travelled a distance of 9.9 m. Calculate the average speed of the car during the first 3.0s of the journey. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

Average speed is calculated as (total distance) ⁄ (total time). So, 9.9 m ⁄ 3.0 s = 3.3 m/s.

(iii) On Fig. 1.1, sketch a distance-time graph for the first 3.0s of the journey. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

The graph should be a curve starting from the origin with an increasing gradient, passing through the point (3.0 s, 9.9 m).

Question 4

(0625/41_Summer_2017_Q2) - Forces And Motion, Forces And Energy

A footballer kicks a ball vertically upwards. Initially, the ball is stationary.

(a) His boot is in contact with the ball for 0.050s. The average resultant force on the ball during this time is 180N. The ball leaves his foot at 20 m/s.

Calculate

(i) the impulse of the force acting on the ball, [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Impulse is calculated as Force × time. So, 180 N × 0.050 s gives an impulse of 9.0 Ns.

(ii) the mass of the ball, [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Impulse equals the change in momentum (Ft = mv). Mass is m = Ft ⁄ v. So, 9.0 Ns ⁄ 20 m/s = 0.45 kg.

(iii) the height to which the ball rises. Ignore air resistance. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

The initial kinetic energy is converted to gravitational potential energy (½mv² = mgh). The height is h = v² ⁄ (2g) = (20 m/s)² ⁄ (2 × 10 N/kg) = 20 m.

(b) While the boot is in contact with the ball, the ball is no longer spherical. State the word used to describe the energy stored in the ball. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

The energy stored is elastic potential energy or strain energy.

Question 5

(0625/42_Summer_2017_Q2) - Forces And Motion, Forces And Pressure

Fig. 2.1 shows a vehicle designed to be used on the Moon.

The brakes of the vehicle are tested on Earth.

(a) The acceleration of free fall on the Moon is one sixth (1⁄6) of its value on Earth. Tick one box in each column of the table to predict the value of that quantity when the vehicle is used on the Moon, compared to the test on Earth. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

Mass of vehicle on Moon: same as value on Earth.

Weight of vehicle on Moon: 1⁄6 × value on Earth.

Deceleration of vehicle on Moon with same braking force: same as value on Earth.

(b) Fig. 2.2 shows the brake pedal of the vehicle. The driver exerts a force on the pedal, which increases the pressure in the oil to operate the brakes. The area of the piston in the cylinder is 6.5 x 10-4 m² (0.00065 m²). The pressure increase in the oil is 5.0 x 105 Pa (500000 Pa). Calculate the force exerted by the driver on the brake pedal. [4]

Tap to reveal answer

First, find the force on the piston: F = P × A = 5.0 × 105 Pa × 6.5 × 10-4 m² = 325 N. Then, using the principle of moments about the pivot, Driver's Force × 24 cm = 325 N × 7.0 cm. The driver's force is (325 × 7.0) ⁄ 24 = 95 N.

Question 6

(0625/43_Summer_2017_Q2) - Forces And Motion, Forces And Energy

(a) State the word equation that defines momentum. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

momentum = mass × velocity

(b) A metal block A, travelling in a straight line at 4.0 m/s on a smooth surface, collides with a second metal block B which is at rest. Fig. 2.1 shows the two metal blocks A and B before and after the collision. The mass of A is 3.2 kg. The mass of B is 1.6 kg. After the collision, the velocity of A is 1.5 m/s.

Calculate

(i) the momentum of A before the collision, [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Momentum is p = mv. So, 3.2 kg × 4.0 m/s = 12.8 kg m/s (rounded to 13 in mark scheme).

(ii) the velocity v of B after the collision. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

By conservation of momentum, total momentum before = total momentum after. 12.8 = (3.2 × 1.5) + (1.6 × v). This gives 12.8 = 4.8 + 1.6v. So, 1.6v = 8.0, and v = 5.0 m/s.

(c) In the collision that occurred in (b), block A and block B are in contact for 0.050 s. Calculate the average force that is exerted on B during the collision. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

The force is the rate of change of momentum of block B. F = Δp ⁄ Δt = (1.6 kg × 5.0 m/s) ⁄ 0.050 s = 8.0 ⁄ 0.050 = 160 N.

(d) After the collision in (b), the total kinetic energy of the two blocks is less than the kinetic energy of block A before the collision. Suggest one reason for this. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

Some of the kinetic energy was converted into other forms, such as thermal energy (internal energy) or sound energy during the collision.

Question 7

(0625/41_Summer_2017_Q3) - Forces And Motion

Fig. 3.1 shows remote sensing equipment on the surface of a distant planet.

(a) The mass of the equipment is 350kg. The acceleration of free fall on the surface of this planet is 7.5 m/s².

(i) State what is meant by the term weight. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

Weight is the force of gravity acting on an object.

(ii) Calculate the weight of the equipment on the planet. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Weight is calculated as W = mg. So, 350 kg × 7.5 m/s² = 2625 N (rounded to 2600 N in mark scheme).

(b) The equipment releases a balloon from a point that is a small distance above the surface of the planet. The atmosphere at the surface of this planet has a density of 0.35 kg/m³. The inflated balloon has a mass of 80 g and a volume of 0.30 m³. Make an appropriate calculation and then predict and explain the direction of any motion of the balloon. Show your working. [4]

Tap to reveal answer

Calculation: The density of the balloon is ρ = m ⁄ V = 0.080 kg ⁄ 0.30 m³ = 0.27 kg/m³.

Prediction: The balloon will move up.

Explanation: The balloon moves up because its average density (0.27 kg/m³) is less than the density of the surrounding atmosphere (0.35 kg/m³).

Question 8

(0625/42_Summer_2017_Q3) - Forces And Motion, Forces And Energy

(a) Underline the pair of quantities which must be multiplied together to calculate impulse. [1]

force and mass     time and velocity     force and velocity     weight and velocity     mass and time     force and time

Tap to reveal answer

The correct pair is force and time.

(b) Fig. 3.1 shows a collision between two blocks A and B on a smooth, horizontal surface. Before the collision, block A, of mass 2.4kg, is moving at 3.0 m/s. Block B, of mass 1.2kg, is at rest. After the collision, blocks A and B stick together and move with velocity v.

(i) Calculate

1. the momentum of block A before the collision, [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Momentum is p = mv. So, 2.4kg × 3.0m/s = 7.2 kg m/s.

2. the velocity v, [2]

Tap to reveal answer

By conservation of momentum, mₐuₐ = (mₐ+mₑ)v. So, 7.2 = (2.4 + 1.2)v. This gives v = 7.2 ⁄ 3.6 = 2.0 m/s.

3. the impulse experienced by block B during the collision. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Impulse is the change in momentum of block B. Impulse = m(v-u) = 1.2 kg × (2.0 - 0) m/s = 2.4 Ns.

(ii) Suggest why the total kinetic energy of blocks A and B after the collision is less than the kinetic energy of block A before the collision. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

Energy was converted into other forms, such as thermal energy or sound energy, during the inelastic collision.

IGCSE Physics - Chapter 2: Forces and Motion (Questions 9-16)

Question 9

(0625/41_Winter_2017_Q1) - Forces And Motion

Fig. 1.1 shows the speed-time graph for the motion of a car.

The mass of the car is 1200 kg.

(a) Calculate, for the first 20s of the motion,

(i) the distance travelled by the car, [2]

Tap to reveal answer

The distance is the area under the graph. For the first 20s, this is a triangle with area ½ × base × height = ½ × 20 s × 13 m/s = 130 m.

(ii) the acceleration of the car, [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Acceleration is the gradient of the graph. a = (v-u) ⁄ t = (13 m/s - 0 m/s) ⁄ 20 s = 0.65 m/s².

(iii) the resultant force acting on the car. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Resultant force is calculated using F = ma. So, 1200 kg × 0.65 m/s² = 780 N.

(b) Describe the motion of the car in the period of time from 25s to 40s. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

The car is accelerating, but the rate of acceleration is decreasing. The speed is increasing at a lower rate.

Question 10

(0625/43_Winter_2017_Q1) - Forces And Motion

A truck accelerates uniformly along a straight, horizontal road. The mass of the truck is 2.0 x 104 kg.

(a) The speed of the truck increases from rest to 12m/s in 30 s. Calculate

(i) the distance travelled by the truck during this time, [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Distance can be calculated using s = average speed × time = ((u+v) ⁄ 2) × t. So, ((0+12) ⁄ 2) × 30 = 180 m.

(ii) the resultant force on the truck. [4]

Tap to reveal answer

First, calculate acceleration: a = Δv ⁄ t = 12 m/s ⁄ 30 s = 0.40 m/s². Then, calculate force: F = ma = (2.0 × 104 kg) × 0.40 m/s² = 8000 N.

(b) To maintain a uniform acceleration, the forward force on the truck must change. Explain why. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

As the speed of the truck increases, the resistive force of air resistance (or drag) increases. To maintain a constant resultant force (and thus constant acceleration), the forward engine force must increase to counteract the growing resistive force.

Question 11

(0625/42_Winter_2017_Q2) - Forces And Motion

(a) An object is moving in a straight line at constant speed. A resultant force begins to act upon the object. State the ways in which the force may change the motion of the object. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

The force can cause the object to accelerate (increase speed), decelerate (decrease speed), stop, or change direction.

(b) State one other effect a force could have on the object. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

A force could also cause a change of shape or size.

(c) The mass of a car is 1400kg. The car, initially at rest, is moved along a level road by a resultant force of 3500 N. The car reaches a speed of 30 m/s.

(i) Calculate the average acceleration of the car. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Using F=ma, the acceleration is a = F ⁄ m = 3500 N ⁄ 1400 kg = 2.5 m/s².

(ii) Calculate the time for which the force is applied. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Using a = (v-u) ⁄ t, the time is t = (v-u) ⁄ a = (30 m/s - 0) ⁄ 2.5 m/s² = 12 s.

(iii) State the name of a force which opposes the motion of the car. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

A force opposing the motion is friction or air resistance (drag).

Question 12

(0625/41_Winter_2017_Q4) - Forces And Motion, Forces And Pressure

Fig. 4.1 shows a balloon filled with helium that is used to lift measuring instruments to a great height above the Earth's surface.

(a) Explain, in terms of momentum, how the atoms of helium produce a force on the wall of the balloon. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

Helium atoms collide with the wall of the balloon and rebound. This causes a change of momentum for the atoms. The force on the wall is equal to the total rate of change of momentum of the atoms.

(b) At ground level, the pressure of the helium in the balloon is 1.0 x 105 Pa. The volume occupied by the helium is 9.6m³. The balloon is released and it rises quickly through the atmosphere. The volume occupied by the helium increases, but the temperature of the helium may be assumed to stay constant.

(i) Explain, in terms of the helium atoms in the balloon, why the pressure in the balloon is smaller than at ground level. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

As the volume increases, there are fewer atoms per unit volume. This leads to a lower rate of collision of atoms with the walls of the balloon, resulting in lower pressure.

(ii) Calculate the pressure of the helium when it occupies a volume of 12m³. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Assuming constant temperature, Boyle's Law applies: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂. So, P₂ = P₁V₁ ⁄ V₂ = (1.0 × 105 Pa × 9.6 m³) ⁄ 12 m³ = 8.0 x 104 Pa.

Question 13

(0625/41_Summer_2018_Q1) - Forces And Motion

Fig. 1.1 shows the speed-time graph for a vehicle accelerating from rest.

(a) Calculate the acceleration of the vehicle at time t = 30s. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

The acceleration is the gradient of the graph at that point. By drawing a tangent to the curve at t = 30s and calculating its gradient (change in speed ⁄ change in time), the acceleration is found to be in the range of 0.30 to 0.45 m/s².

(b) Without further calculation, state how the acceleration at time t = 100s compares to the acceleration at time t = 10s. Suggest, in terms of force, a reason why any change has taken place. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

The acceleration at t=100s is less than at t=10s. This is because as speed increases, resistive forces like air resistance increase. This causes the resultant force on the vehicle to decrease, leading to a smaller acceleration.

(c) Determine the distance travelled by the vehicle between time t = 120s and time t = 160s. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

The distance is the area under the graph. This section is a trapezium. Area = ½ × (sum of parallel sides) × height = ½ × (30 m/s + 20 m/s) × 40 s = 1000 m.

Question 14

(0625/42_Summer_2018_Q1) - Forces And Motion

(a) Fig. 1.1 shows the axes of a distance-time graph for an object moving in a straight line.

(i) 1. On Fig. 1.1, draw between time = 0 and time = 10s, the graph for an object moving with a constant speed of 5.0 m/s. Start your graph at distance = 0m. [2]

2. State the property of the graph that represents speed.

Tap to reveal answer

1. The graph is a straight line from (0,0) to (10s, 50m).

2. The property representing speed is the gradient (or slope) of the graph.

(ii) Between time = 10s and time = 20s the object accelerates. The speed at time = 20s is 9.0 m/s. Calculate the average acceleration between time = 10s and time = 20 s. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Average acceleration is a = (v-u) ⁄ t. The initial speed at 10s was 5.0 m/s. So, a = (9.0 m/s - 5.0 m/s) ⁄ 10 s = 0.40 m/s².

(b) Fig. 1.2 shows the axes of a speed-time graph for a different object.

(i) The object has an initial speed of 50 m/s and decelerates uniformly at 0.35 m/s² for 100 s. On Fig. 1.2, draw the graph to represent the motion of the object. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

The graph should be a straight line starting from (0s, 50m/s) and ending at (100s, 15m/s), since the speed decrease is 0.35 m/s² × 100 s = 35 m/s.

(ii) Calculate the distance travelled by the object from time = 0 to time = 100s. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

The distance is the area under the graph. Area of trapezium = ½ × (50 + 15) × 100 = 3250 m (The mark scheme gives 3300m, likely a slight calculation variance or rounding).

Question 15

(0625/43_Summer_2018_Q1) - Forces And Motion

There is no atmosphere on the Moon. A space probe is launched from the surface of the Moon. Fig. 1.1 shows the speed-time graph of the space probe.

(a) Determine the acceleration of the space probe at time = 0. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

The acceleration at t=0 is the initial gradient of the curve. By drawing a tangent at the origin and calculating its slope, the value is found to be in the range of 13 to 14 m/s².

(b) Between time = 0 and time = 150s, the acceleration of the space probe changes.

(i) Without calculation, state how the graph shows this. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

The graph shows the acceleration is changing because the gradient changes; the graph is curved.

(ii) During this time, the thrust exerted on the space probe by the motor remains constant. State one possible reason why the acceleration changes in the way shown by Fig. 1.1. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

The acceleration increases because the mass of the space rocket decreases as it burns and ejects fuel. A constant thrust on a decreasing mass results in increasing acceleration (from F=ma).

(c) Calculate the distance travelled by the space probe from time = 200 s to time = 300 s. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

The distance is the area under the graph. This section is a trapezium. Area = ½ × (4100 m/s + 5000 m/s) × 100 s = 4.55 x 105 m.

Question 16

(0625/41_Winter_2018_Q1) - Forces And Motion

A train of mass 5.6 x 105 kg is at rest in a station. At time t = 0 s, a resultant force acts on the train and it starts to accelerate forwards. Fig. 1.1 is the distance-time graph for the train for the first 120s.

(a) (i) Use Fig. 1.1 to determine:

1. the average speed of the train during the 120s [1]

Tap to reveal answer

Average speed = total distance ⁄ total time = 4800 m ⁄ 120 s = 40 m/s.

2. the speed of the train at time t = 100s. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

The speed at t=100s is the gradient of the tangent to the curve at that point. The graph is a straight line after approx 80s, so we can take the gradient of this line. The value is between 50 and 60 m/s.

(ii) Describe how the acceleration of the train at time t = 100s differs from the acceleration at time t = 20s. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

At t = 20s, the graph is curving, so the speed is changing and there is a positive acceleration. At t = 100s, the graph is a straight line, meaning the speed is constant and the acceleration is zero.

(b) (i) The initial acceleration of the train is 0.75 m/s². Calculate the resultant force that acts on the train at this time. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Resultant force is F = ma = (5.6 × 105 kg) × 0.75 m/s² = 4.2 x 105 N.

(ii) At time t = 120s, the train begins to decelerate. State what is meant by deceleration. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

Deceleration is a decrease in speed/velocity over time, or a negative acceleration.

IGCSE Physics - Chapter 2: Forces and Motion (Questions 17-24)

Question 17

(0625/42_Winter_2018_Q1) - Forces And Motion

A lorry is travelling along a straight, horizontal road.

Fig. 1.1 is the distance-time graph for the lorry.

(a) Using Fig. 1.1, determine:

(i) the speed of the lorry at time t = 30 s [2]

Tap to reveal answer

The speed is the gradient of the distance-time graph. In the first 60 seconds, the graph is a straight line. The gradient is calculated as (change in distance) ⁄ (change in time) = 1800 m ⁄ 60 s, which gives a speed of 30 m/s.

(ii) the average speed of the lorry between time t = 60 s and time t = 120s. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Average speed is calculated as (total distance travelled) ⁄ (total time taken). Between 60s and 120s, the distance travelled is 2700 m - 1800 m = 900 m. The time taken is 60s. So, the average speed is 900 m ⁄ 60 s = 15 m/s.

(b) At time t = 30s, the total resistive force acting on the lorry is 1.4 x 104 N.

(i) Using Fig. 1.1, determine the magnitude of the acceleration of the lorry at time t = 30 s. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

At t = 30 s, the lorry is moving at a constant speed (the graph is a straight line). Therefore, the magnitude of the acceleration is 0 m/s².

(ii) Determine the forward force on the lorry due to its engine at time t = 30 s. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Since the acceleration is zero, the resultant force is zero. This means the forward force from the engine is equal and opposite to the total resistive force. The forward force is 1.4 x 104 N.

(c) Describe the motion of the lorry between time t = 60s and time t = 130s. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

Between 60s and approximately 110s, the lorry's speed is decreasing (it is decelerating). After that, the distance-time graph becomes horizontal, indicating that the lorry is stationary (speed is zero).

Question 18

(0625/43_Winter_2018_Q1) - Forces And Motion

Fig. 1.1 is the distance-time graph for a moving car.

(a) On Fig. 1.1, mark a point P where the acceleration of the car is zero. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

Point P should be marked on the straight-line section of the graph (between t=0 and t=30s), as a constant gradient on a distance-time graph indicates constant speed and therefore zero acceleration.

(b) Determine:

(i) the speed of the car at time t = 15s [2]

Tap to reveal answer

The speed is the gradient of the graph. For the first 30s, the gradient is constant: (150 m) ⁄ (30 s) = 5.0 m/s.

(ii) the average speed of the car between time t = 30s and time t = 45s. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Average speed is calculated as (change in distance) ⁄ (change in time). This is (300 m - 150 m) ⁄ (45 s - 30 s) = 150 m ⁄ 15 s = 10 m/s.

(c) At time t = 45 s, the car starts to decelerate. At time t = 55 s and at a distance of 400 m from the starting point, the car stops. It then remains stationary for 5.0s. On Fig. 1.1, draw a possible continuation of the distance-time graph. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

The graph should show a curve with a decreasing gradient from (45s, 300m) to (55s, 400m). Then, a horizontal line should be drawn from (55s, 400m) to (60s, 400m) to show the car is stationary.

Question 19

(0625/43_Winter_2018_Q2) - Forces And Motion, Forces And Energy

(a) Complete Fig. 2.1 by writing in the right-hand column the name of the quantity given by the product in the left-hand column. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

mass × acceleration = force

force × time = impulse

(b) Fig. 2.2 shows a man hitting a ball with a golf club.

The ball has a mass of 0.046kg. The golf club is in contact with the ball for 5.0 x 10-4s and the ball leaves the golf club at a speed of 65 m/s.

(i) Calculate:

1. the momentum of the ball as it leaves the golf club [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Momentum is calculated as p = mv. So, 0.046 kg × 65 m/s gives a momentum of 3.0 kg m/s.

2. the average resultant force acting on the ball while it is in contact with the golf club. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

The average force is the change in momentum divided by time, F = Δp ⁄ t. So, 3.0 kg m/s ⁄ (5.0 × 10-4 s) gives an average force of 6000 N.

(ii) While the golf club is in contact with the ball, the ball becomes compressed and changes shape. State the type of energy stored in the ball during its contact with the golf club. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

The energy stored due to the compression is elastic potential energy or strain energy.

Question 20

(0625/42_Winter_2018_Q3) - Forces And Motion, Forces And Energy

(a) The velocity of an object of mass m increases from u to v. State, in terms of m, u and v, the change of momentum of the object. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

The change in momentum is given by the expression mv - mu.

(b) In a game of tennis, a player hits a stationary ball with his racquet.

(i) The racquet is in contact with the ball for 6.0ms. The average force on the ball during this time is 400N. Calculate the impulse on the tennis ball. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Impulse is calculated as force × time. So, 400 N × 0.0060 s gives an impulse of 2.4 Ns.

(ii) The mass of the ball is 0.056kg. Calculate the speed with which the ball leaves the racquet. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Since impulse equals the change in momentum (Ft = mv - mu) and the ball starts from rest (u=0), the final speed is v = Ft ⁄ m. This is 2.4 Ns ⁄ 0.056 kg, which is 43 m/s.

(iii) State the energy transfer that takes place:

1. as the ball changes shape during the contact between the racquet and the ball

Tap to reveal answer

The energy transfer is from kinetic energy of the racquet to elastic potential energy in the ball and strings.

2. as the ball leaves the racquet.

Tap to reveal answer

The energy transfer is from elastic potential energy back into kinetic energy of the ball.

Question 21

(0625/41_Summer_2019_Q1) - Forces And Motion

A rocket is stationary on the launchpad. At time t = 0, the rocket engines are switched on and exhaust gases are ejected from the nozzles of the engines. The rocket accelerates upwards.

Fig. 1.1 shows how the acceleration of the rocket varies between time t = 0 and time t = tf.

(a) Define acceleration. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, or the change of velocity ⁄ unit time.

(b) On Fig. 1.2, sketch a graph to show how the speed of the rocket varies between time t = 0 and time t = tf. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

The graph should start at the origin. Since the acceleration is initially increasing, the speed graph will be a curve with an increasing gradient. When the acceleration becomes constant, the speed graph will become a straight line with a constant positive gradient.

(c) Some time later, the rocket is far from the Earth. The effect of the Earth's gravity on the motion of the rocket is insignificant. As the rocket accelerates, its momentum increases.

(i) State the principle of the conservation of momentum. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

In an isolated system where no external forces act, the total momentum remains constant.

(ii) Explain how the principle of the conservation of momentum applies to the accelerating rocket and the exhaust gases. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

The total momentum of the rocket-gas system is initially zero. As the rocket ejects gas, the gas gains momentum in one direction (downwards). To conserve momentum, the rocket gains an equal amount of momentum in the opposite direction (upwards), causing it to accelerate.

Question 22

(0625/42_Summer_2019_Q1) - Forces And Motion

A bus is travelling between points A and D. There are bus stops at A, B, C and D but the bus does not stop at B and C. Fig. 1.1 is a speed-time graph for the bus.

(a) Describe the motion of the bus between each of the bus stops. Select the appropriate description from the list below. [3]

constant acceleration, increasing acceleration, decreasing acceleration, moving backwards at constant speed, moving forwards at constant speed, stationary

Tap to reveal answer

1. between A and B: decreasing acceleration

2. between B and C: moving forwards at constant speed

3. between C and D: constant deceleration (negative acceleration)

(b) The average speed of the bus between A and D is 23 km/h. Calculate the distance between A and D. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

Distance is calculated as average speed × time. The total time from A to D is 2.0 minutes, which is 2.0 ⁄ 60 hours. So, the distance is 23 km/h × (2.0 ⁄ 60) h = 0.77 km.

(c) The bus stops at D for 1 min and then travels at a constant acceleration for 30 seconds. On Fig. 1.1, sketch a possible graph for this additional motion. Label X when the bus starts to accelerate and label Y for 30 seconds later. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

A horizontal line should be drawn at speed = 0 from t = 2.0 min to t = 3.0 min. Point X is at (3.0, 0). From X, a straight line with a constant positive gradient should be drawn for 30 seconds (to t = 3.5 min). Point Y is at the end of this line.

(0625/43_Summer_2019_Q1) - Forces And Motion

Fig. 1.1 shows a distance-time graph for a cyclist travelling between points P and V on a straight road.

(a) Describe the motion between: Q and R, R and S, S and T. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

Q and R: The gradient is positive and the line is straight, indicating constant velocity/speed.

R and S: The gradient is decreasing, indicating deceleration.

S and T: The graph is horizontal, indicating the cyclist is stationary.

(b) Calculate the speed between P and R. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

The speed is the gradient of the graph between P and R. From the graph, this is 160 m ⁄ 100 s = 1.6 m/s.

(c) After point V, the straight road continues down a steep hill. The cyclist travels down the steep hill. He does not apply the brakes and all resistive forces can be ignored. On Fig. 1.1, sketch a possible motion for the cyclist after V. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

Question 24

(0625/42_Summer_2019_Q2) - Forces And Motion

Fig. 2.1 shows a model fire engine. Its brakes are applied. 0.80 kg of water is emitted in the jet every 6.0s at a velocity of 0.72 m/s relative to the engine.

(a) Calculate the change in momentum of the water that is ejected in 6.0s. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

The change in momentum is calculated as Δp = mΔv. So, 0.80 kg × 0.72 m/s gives a change in momentum of 0.58 kg m/s.

(b) Calculate the magnitude of the force acting on the model because of the jet of water. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Force is the rate of change of momentum, F = Δp ⁄ t. So, 0.58 kg m/s ⁄ 6.0 s gives a force of 0.096 N.

(c) The brakes of the model are released. State and explain the direction of the acceleration of the model. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Statement: The model accelerates to the right (backwards).

Explanation: A force is exerted on the water to eject it to the left. By Newton's third law, the water exerts an equal and opposite force on the model, pushing it to the right. Acceleration is in the same direction as the resultant force.

(d) In (c) the model contains a water tank, which is initially full. State and explain any change in the magnitude of the initial acceleration if the brakes are first released when the tank is nearly empty. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

Statement: The acceleration will be more when the tank is empty.

Explanation: The force from the water jet remains constant. When the tank is empty, the total mass of the model is less. According to Newton's second law (F=ma), for a constant force, a smaller mass results in a greater acceleration.

IGCSE Physics - Chapter 2: Forces and Motion (Questions 25-32)

Question 25

(0625/43_Summer_2019_Q2) - Forces And Motion, Forces And Energy

Fig. 2.1 is the top view of a small ship of mass 1.2 x 106 kg. The ship is moving slowly sideways at 0.040 m/s as it comes in to dock.

The ship hits the wooden pillars which move towards the dock wall.

(a) Calculate the kinetic energy of the ship before it hits the pillars. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Kinetic energy is calculated using the formula KE = ½mv². So, KE = ½ × (1.2 × 106 kg) × (0.040 m/s)², which equals 960 J.

(b) The ship is in contact with the pillars for 0.30s as it comes to rest. Calculate the average force exerted on the side of the ship. [4]

Tap to reveal answer

First, calculate the change in momentum (impulse): Δp = mv = (1.2 × 106 kg) × (0.040 m/s) = 4.8 × 104 kg m/s. Then, the average force is F = Δp ⁄ t = (4.8 × 104 kg m/s) ⁄ 0.30 s, which equals 1.6 x 105 N.

(c) Assume that the kinetic energy calculated in (a) is used to do work moving the pillars. Calculate the distance moved by the pillars. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Work done is equal to the force multiplied by the distance moved (Work Done = Fd). The work done is equal to the initial kinetic energy of the ship, 960 J. The distance is d = Work ⁄ F = 960 J ⁄ (1.6 × 105 N) = 0.0060 m or 6.0 mm.

(d) Dock walls sometimes have the pillars replaced with rubber car tyres. Explain how this reduces the possibility of damage when a boat docks. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

The rubber tyres are compressible, which increases the time of collision. Since the change in momentum is the same, increasing the time over which the force acts results in a smaller average force exerted on both the ship and the dock wall, reducing the chance of damage.

Question 26

(0625/41_Winter_2019_Q1) - Forces And Motion

A car accelerates from rest at time t=0 to its maximum speed.

Fig. 1.1 is the speed-time graph for the first 25 s of its motion.

(a) The mass of the car is 2300 kg. For the time between t=0 and t=5.0 s, determine:

(i) the acceleration of the car [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Acceleration is the gradient of the speed-time graph. Between 0 and 5.0 s, the graph is a straight line. The acceleration is a = Δv ⁄ Δt = (15 m/s) ⁄ (5.0 s) = 3.0 m/s².

(ii) the resultant force acting on the car. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Resultant force is calculated using F = ma. So, F = 2300 kg × 3.0 m/s², which equals 6900 N.

(b) Describe the motion of the car between t=10s and t=15s. Explain how Fig. 1.1 shows this. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

Between 10s and 15s, the car is still accelerating but at a decreasing rate. The graph shows this because the speed is increasing, but the gradient of the graph is positive and decreasing.

(c) Between t=10s and t=15 s, the force exerted on the car due to the engine remains constant. Suggest and explain why the car moves in the way shown by Fig. 1.1. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

As the car's speed increases, the resistive force of air resistance also increases. With a constant engine force, the increasing resistive force causes the resultant force to decrease, which in turn causes the acceleration to decrease.

Question 27

(0625/41_Winter_2019_Q3) - Forces And Motion

Fig. 3.1 shows a shooting competition, where air rifles fire soft metal pellets at distant targets.

When an air rifle is fired, it exerts an impulse of 0.019 Ns on the pellet.

(a) Define impulse. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

Impulse is the product of the force and the time for which it acts.

(b) The pellet has a mass of 1.1 x 10-4 kg. Determine:

(i) the speed with which the pellet leaves the air rifle [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Impulse is equal to the change in momentum (I = mv, since it starts from rest). So, the speed is v = I ⁄ m = 0.019 Ns ⁄ (1.1 × 10-4 kg), which is approximately 170 m/s.

(ii) the kinetic energy of the pellet as it leaves the rifle. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

Kinetic energy is calculated as KE = ½mv². So, KE = ½ × (1.1 × 10-4 kg) × (170 m/s)², which is approximately 1.6 J.

(c) The pellet melts when it strikes the target. Describe how the molecular structure of the liquid metal differs from that of the solid metal. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

In a liquid, the molecules have an irregular or random arrangement, are further apart on average, and are not fixed in place, allowing them to move past each other. In a solid, molecules are typically in a fixed, regular pattern.

Question 28

(0625/41_Summer_2020_Q1) - Forces And Motion

An aeroplane of mass 2.5 x 105 kg lands with a speed of 62 m/s, on a horizontal runway at time t=0. The aeroplane decelerates uniformly as it travels along the runway in a straight line until it reaches a speed of 6.0 m/s at t=35 s.

(a) Calculate:

(i) the deceleration of the aeroplane in the 35 s after it lands [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Deceleration is calculated using a = (v-u) ⁄ t. So, a = (6.0 m/s - 62 m/s) ⁄ 35 s = -1.6 m/s². The deceleration is 1.6 m/s².

(ii) the resultant force acting on the aeroplane as it decelerates [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Resultant force is F = ma = (2.5 × 105 kg) × 1.6 m/s², which equals 4.0 x 105 N.

(iii) the momentum of the aeroplane when its speed is 6.0 m/s [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Momentum is p = mv = (2.5 × 105 kg) × 6.0 m/s, which equals 1.5 x 106 kg m/s.

(b) At t=35 s, the aeroplane stops decelerating and moves along the runway at a constant speed of 6.0 m/s for a further 15s. On Fig. 1.1, sketch the shape of the graph for the distance travelled by the aeroplane along the runway between t=0 and t=50 s. You are not required to calculate distance values. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

The distance-time graph from t=0 to t=35s should be a curve with a decreasing gradient, starting from the origin. From t=35s to t=50s, the speed is constant, so the graph should be a straight line with a positive gradient.

(c) As the aeroplane decelerates, its kinetic energy decreases. Suggest what happens to this energy. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

The kinetic energy is converted primarily into thermal energy in the brakes, tyres, and the surrounding air due to work done against friction.

Question 29

(0625/42_Summer_2020_Q1) - Forces And Motion

Fig. 1.1 shows the speed-time graph of a person on a journey. On the journey, he walks and then waits for a bus. He then travels by bus. He gets off the bus and waits for two minutes. He then walks again. His journey takes 74 minutes.

(a) For the whole journey calculate:

(i) the distance travelled [3]

Tap to reveal answer

The total distance is the total area under the speed-time graph. By calculating the area of each section (walking, bus travel, final walk) and adding them together, the total distance is found to be 17 km.

(ii) the average speed. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Average speed is total distance ⁄ total time. The total time is 74 minutes. So, the average speed is 17 km ⁄ (74 ⁄ 60) h, which is approximately 14 km/h.

(b) State and explain which feature of a speed-time graph shows acceleration. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

The gradient of the graph shows acceleration. The gradient is calculated as the change of speed divided by time.

(c) State and explain the acceleration of the person at time = 40 minutes. [2]

(0625/43_Summer_2020_Q1) - Forces And Motion

(a) Define acceleration. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity.

(b) Fig. 1.1 shows two speed-time graphs, A and B, and two distance-time graphs, C and D.

Describe the motion shown by:

(i) graph A [2]

Question 31

(0625/42_Summer_2020_Q2) - Forces And Motion

Fig. 2.1 shows a train. The total mass of the train and its passengers is 750000 kg. The train is travelling at a speed of 84 m/s. The driver applies the brakes and the train takes 80s to slow down to a speed of 42 m/s.

(a) Calculate the impulse applied to the train as it slows down. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

Impulse is the change in momentum, calculated as impulse = m(v-u). The change in momentum is 750000 kg × (42 m/s - 84 m/s), which equals a magnitude of 3.2 x 107 Ns.

(b) Calculate the average resultant force applied to the train as it slows down. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

The average resultant force is the impulse divided by time (F = Impulse ⁄ t). So, (3.2 × 107 Ns) ⁄ 80 s gives a force of 3.9 x 105 N.

(c) Suggest how the shape of the train helps it to travel at high speeds. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

A streamlined or aerodynamic shape reduces air resistance (drag), allowing it to maintain high speeds more efficiently.

(d) The train took 80s to reduce its speed from 84 m/s to 42m/s. Explain why, with the same braking force, the train takes more than 80s to reduce its speed from 42 m/s to zero. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

The total resistive force is the braking force plus air resistance. At lower speeds, there is less air resistance. With the same braking force, the total resultant decelerating force is smaller, so it takes a longer time to produce the same change in speed.

(e) On a wet day, the train travels a greater distance before it stops along the same track. The train has the same speed of 84 m/s before the brakes are applied. Suggest a reason for this. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

On a wet day, the friction between the train's wheels and the rails is reduced. This reduces the maximum possible braking force, leading to a smaller deceleration and a longer stopping distance.

Question 32

(0625/43_Summer_2020_Q3) - Forces And Pressure, Forces And Motion

In a double-decker bus there are two passenger compartments, one above the other.

(a) Fig. 3.1 shows a double-decker bus on a tilted platform. The platform is used to test the stability of the bus. The angle the bus makes with the horizontal is gradually increased until the bus begins to topple to the left. Explain why the bus begins to topple. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

The bus begins to topple when the vertical line of action of its weight, acting through the centre of mass, falls outside the base of the bus. This creates an unbalanced moment that causes it to rotate and fall over.

(b) There are 30 passengers in the upper compartment of the bus and 2 passengers in the bottom compartment of the bus. State how this affects the stability of the bus and the reason for this. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

This makes the bus less stable. The reason is that having more mass in the upper compartment raises the overall centre of mass of the bus, making it easier to topple.

(c) A bus is travelling along a straight road. The bus and the driver have a combined mass of 16000kg when there are no passengers in it. The bus has 73 passengers. The average mass of each of the passengers is 65kg.

(i) Calculate the total mass of the bus, the driver and the 73 passengers. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

The total mass is the sum of the bus's mass and the passengers' mass. Mass of passengers = 73 × 65 kg = 4745 kg. Total mass = 16000 kg + 4745 kg = 20745 kg (rounded to 21000 kg in the scheme).

(ii) The fully loaded bus accelerates uniformly from rest to a speed of 14 m/s. The time taken to reach a speed of 14 m/s is 20s. Calculate the resultant force on the bus during the acceleration. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

First, calculate acceleration: a = Δv ⁄ t = 14 m/s ⁄ 20 s = 0.70 m/s². Then, using F = ma with the total mass, F = 21000 kg × 0.70 m/s², the resultant force is 15000 N (rounded).

Tap to reveal answer

The impulse is equal to the change in momentum. The magnitude of the impulse is 3.0 Ns, and its direction is 45° to the original direction.

(ii) Determine the magnitude of the new momentum of the disc and its new direction relative to the original direction of travel by drawing a scale diagram. [4]

Question 34

(0625/42_Winter_2020_Q1) - Forces And Motion

A sky-diver jumps out of a hot-air balloon, which is 4000 m above the ground. At time = 30 s, she opens her parachute.

Fig. 1.1 is the speed-time graph of her fall.

(a) (i) Label with the letter X the point on the graph where the sky-diver opens her parachute. [1]

(ii) Label with the letters Y and Z the two parts of the graph where the sky-diver falls at terminal velocity. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

(i) Point X should be labelled at t = 30 s, where the graph shows a sudden, large deceleration.

(ii) Points Y and Z should be labelled on the horizontal sections of the graph, where the speed is constant (one before opening the parachute, one after).

(b) Describe, in terms of the forces acting on the sky-diver, her motion between leaving the balloon and opening her parachute. [4]

Tap to reveal answer

Initially, the only significant force is weight, causing downward acceleration. As speed increases, air resistance increases, opposing the motion. The resultant downward force decreases, so acceleration decreases. Eventually, air resistance becomes equal to weight, the resultant force is zero, and she falls at a constant terminal velocity.

(c) Calculate the average speed of the sky-diver in the first 4.0s of her fall. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Using the formula for average speed with uniform acceleration, average speed = (initial speed + final speed) ⁄ 2. From the graph, at t=4.0s, the speed is 40 m/s. So, (0 + 40) ⁄ 2 = 20 m/s.

(0625/43_Winter_2020_Q1) - Forces And Motion

(a) Fig. 1.1 shows a trolley travelling down a ramp. The trolley has a piece of paper tape attached to it. The tape passes through a machine which makes a dot on the tape every 0.02s.

Fig. 1.2 shows a section of the tape.

Tap to reveal answer

Description: The trolley accelerates or its speed increases.

Explanation: A greater tilt angle means there is a larger resultant force acting on the trolley down the ramp, causing it to accelerate.

(b) Another trolley is released from the top of the ramp. Fig. 1.3 shows the speed-time graph for this trolley. Using Fig. 1.3, calculate the distance travelled by the trolley in the first 0.5s. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

(0625/41_Winter_2020_Q2) - Forces And Motion, Forces And Energy

(i) Calculate the gravitational potential energy transferred from the ball as it falls. [2]

(0625/43_Winter_2020_Q2) - Forces And Energy, Forces And Motion

Question 39

(0625/41_Summer_2021_Q1) - Forces And Motion

A skydiver of mass 76kg is falling vertically in still air. At time t = 0, the skydiver opens his parachute.

Fig. 1.1 is the speed-time graph for the skydiver from t = 0.

(a) Using Fig. 1.1, determine:

(i) the deceleration of the skydiver immediately after the parachute opens [2]

Tap to reveal answer

The deceleration is the initial gradient of the speed-time graph. Drawing a tangent at t=0 gives a value in the range of 35 to 43 m/s².

(ii) the force due to air resistance acting on the skydiver immediately after the parachute opens. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

The resultant upward force is Fres = ma. The forces acting are weight (down) and air resistance (up). So, Fair - W = ma, which means Fair = ma + W. Using a deceleration of 40 m/s², Fair = (76 kg × 40 m/s²) + (76 kg × 10 N/kg) = 3040 N + 760 N = 3800 N.

(b) Explain, in terms of the forces acting on the skydiver, his motion between t = 0 and t = 6.0 s. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

The upward force (air resistance) is greater than the weight, causing an upward resultant force and thus deceleration. As speed decreases, air resistance decreases, which reduces the resultant upward force and the deceleration. Eventually, the weight equals the air resistance, the resultant force is zero, and the skydiver reaches a new, slower terminal velocity.

(c) Explain why opening the parachute cannot reduce the speed of the skydiver to zero. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Air resistance depends on speed; at zero speed, there is no air resistance. If the skydiver were to stop, the only force acting would be his weight downwards, which would immediately cause him to accelerate downwards again.

Question 40

(0625/42_Summer_2021_Q1) - Measurements And Units, Forces And Motion

(a) Fig. 1.1 shows a sealed weather balloon which is stationary in still air. State whether the overall density of the balloon and its instruments is greater than, less than, or the same as the density of the surrounding air. [1]

The overall density of the balloon is the same as the density of the surrounding air.

(b) At night, the gas inside the balloon cools. The pressure of the air outside the balloon remains the same.

(i) State whether the balloon rises, falls or remains stationary. [1]

Tap to reveal answer

The balloon falls.

(ii) Explain your answer. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

When the gas cools, its volume decreases. Since the mass remains constant, the overall density of the balloon increases. It becomes denser than the surrounding air and therefore sinks.

(c) An object is released from the balloon. It starts at rest and eventually reaches a constant speed.

(i) On the axes of Fig. 1.2, sketch a speed-time graph to show this motion. [3]

Tap to reveal answer

The graph should start at the origin and be a curve with a decreasing gradient that becomes horizontal when it reaches constant speed.

(ii) State the values of the initial acceleration and the final acceleration of the object. [2]

Tap to reveal answer

Initial acceleration = 10 m/s² (acceleration of free fall).

Final acceleration = 0 m/s² (at constant terminal velocity).
